top.headline: A Texas Town Got $100,000 After One Immigration Arrest. It Could Be Worth Millions More.
top.blurb: KXAN and ProPublica found the small North Texas town of Pantego received $100,000 under a federal 287(g) agreement after a single immigration arrest, with its police chief projecting up to $720,000 more — nearly 40% of the town's police budget. Texas now leads the nation with 429 such agreements, and newly elected Democratic state officials are questioning a program that rewards arrests with almost no spending oversight.

top.headline: A Nationwide FAA Ground Stop Grounded 12,000 Flights. A Week Later, No One Can Say Why.
top.blurb: A Nov. 13 ground stop disrupted roughly 12,000 flights and stranded an estimated 1.5 million passengers, and officials still can't say why a week later. The FAA first blamed unstable radar and communications feeds before the FBI seized the equipment on suspicion of a possible hack, while denying its new AI-assisted routing system was responsible. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is using the episode to request $50 billion from Congress, even as critics note the agency hasn't spent money it already has.

top.headline: Democrats Push to Renew Trump's Warrantless Spying Powers Before They Lose Congress
top.blurb: Democratic Rep. Jim Himes and Sen. Mark Warner are pushing to renew Section 702 of FISA during the lame-duck session, before Republicans lose their congressional majorities, even though existing court orders let the warrantless surveillance program continue into March 2027 regardless. Sen. Ron Wyden and privacy advocates are fighting any renewal that doesn't add a warrant requirement, and progressive groups call the rush a betrayal of midterm voters who handed Democrats power partly on a civil-liberties message.

top.headline: India Dismisses US Religious Freedom Panel's Claim It's Deporting Muslims as 'Politically Motivated'
top.blurb: India's foreign ministry dismissed as 'blatantly political' a US religious freedom commission's finding that New Delhi is stripping Muslims from voter rolls and deporting them as 'foreigners,' a charge built on Home Minister Amit Shah's claim that three crore purged voters were Bangladeshi infiltrators. It's the latest clash between Delhi and the commission, days after India's ambassador told it to stop 'lecturing others' over a jailed activist, as the Opposition says the citizenship-revision drive has removed 13 crore voters nationwide.

top.headline: Eleven Dead, Over 180 Hospitalised After Drinking Spurious Liquor in Manipur
top.blurb: Eleven men died and more than 180 people were hospitalised after drinking spurious liquor bought from a neighbouring district in Manipur's Chandel area over two days. Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited hospital wards in Imphal and ordered an inquiry to identify who supplied the alcohol, as authorities warned residents against locally brewed drinks of 'doubtful origin.'

top.headline: Delhi Is Clearing Its 'Green Lungs' With Bulldozers. Even Backers of the Cleanup Call the Method Reckless.
top.blurb: Workers using JCB machinery are clearing invasive trees from Delhi's Central Ridge, the forested 'green lungs' behind Rashtrapati Bhawan, driving over the forest floor and uprooting vegetation well beyond their targets. Environmentalist Pradip Krishen, author of Trees of Delhi, agrees the invasive species need to go but warns that bulldozing and the government's parallel push to 'parkify' the Ridge could damage it for decades.

top.headline: COP31 Climate Talks Blow Past Deadline as Nearly 200 Nations Deadlock Over a Draft That Doesn't Mention Fossil Fuels
top.blurb: Negotiators at the COP31 summit in Türkiye missed Friday's deadline as nearly 200 countries remained split over a draft agreement that dropped all mention of fossil fuels after Saudi Arabia and other producers objected, along with a $120 billion adaptation-funding target. The EU warned the text risks turning the conference into a 'fossil summit,' and Panama has threatened to walk out, as a third draft is expected Saturday with the world already on track to breach the 1.5°C warming limit.

top.headline: US Warns It Will Seize Ships Helping Iran Dodge Its Oil Blockade
top.blurb: US Central Command warned that vessels receiving Iranian crude through ship-to-ship transfers could be seized, diverted or forced into Iranian ports, tightening a naval blockade reinstated in July after a brief ceasefire-era thaw collapsed. Analysts say Iran cannot break the blockade militarily but may try to make it too costly to enforce, with reports that a tanker may be loading Iranian crude for what would be Tehran's first successful export since the blockade resumed.

top.headline: Denmark Expels Russian Diplomat Over Alleged Plot to Assassinate a Ukrainian Rapper
top.blurb: Denmark is expelling Russia's defence attaché after its intelligence service accused Moscow of plotting, with help from a banned local gang, to assassinate Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner at a Copenhagen concert; police intercepted the alleged attackers nearby and found firearms. Two Danish men now face attempted-murder charges, and Copenhagen is weighing a ban on Russian Schengen visas as it links the plot to a wider pattern of Russian sabotage and hybrid attacks across Europe.

top.headline: KL Rahul's Century Headlines India's Dominant Day in Wellington
top.blurb: India piled on 327 runs for three wickets on day three in Wellington to take a 118-run lead, with KL Rahul's 136 — his first Test century in New Zealand — leading a day where all of India's top five batters passed fifty away from home for the first time. Shubman Gill (98), Devdutt Padikkal (80) and an unbeaten Rishabh Pant (55) backed him up as New Zealand's attack struggled to find any breakthrough.

more.headline: The Falkland Islands, ICC's Smallest Member, Win Cricket's First-Ever International Match Held on the Islands
more.blurb: The Falkland Islands, the ICC's smallest member, beat Costa Rica 6-2 in a T20I series at Stanley's Platinum Oval — the first ICC-recognised international match ever held on the islands.

top.headline: 'Being Heumann' Turns a Landmark Disability-Rights Sit-In Into a Vivid, Funny Ensemble Drama
top.blurb: Sian Heder's biographical drama dramatises the 1977 San Francisco sit-in where disability-rights activist Judith Heumann and more than a hundred others forced the government to enforce a landmark disability-discrimination law. Ruth Madeley, who has spina bifida, leads a vivid, often very funny ensemble opposite Mark Ruffalo as the official the activists make impossible to ignore, in what the reviewer calls an inspiring ode to collective protest.

bengal.headline: Cyclone 'Akvan' Dumps Heavy Rain on Bengal, CM Orders District-Wise Crop Damage Reports
bengal.blurb: Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari ordered district-wise crop damage assessments as Cyclone Akvan triggered heavy rain and waterlogging across Kolkata and South Bengal, with more rain forecast through Saturday.

bengal.headline: Bengal Postpones Start of Electoral Roll Revision, Citing 'Unavoidable Circumstances'
bengal.blurb: West Bengal has postponed the November 23 start of its Special Summary Revision of electoral rolls without naming a new date, raising concern that January's final voter list could slip too.

travel.headline: A Rare Rhino Calf Born at Chester Zoo Carries On a Vulnerable Bloodline
travel.blurb: A healthy greater one-horned rhino calf was born at England's Chester Zoo weeks after its father died suddenly, a genetically valuable addition to a species that numbered only 200 in the wild a century ago and has since recovered to roughly 4,000.

happy.headline: George Orwell's Memoir Was Thrown in the Trash. A Friend Fished It Out and Started His Career.
happy.blurb: After Down and Out in Paris and London was rejected twice, a despairing George Orwell threw the manuscript in his friend Mabel's bin — she retrieved it and passed it to an agent, launching his career.

tech_top.headline: Data Centers Are Landing in Black and Hispanic Neighborhoods at More Than Twice the Rate of White Ones, Study Finds
tech_top.blurb: A study of roughly 81,000 census tracts and 5,291 data centers found majority-Black neighborhoods are 2.2 times as likely to host one as white neighborhoods, rising to 4.2 times for majority-Asian neighborhoods, even after controlling for income, education and land costs. Researchers trace much of the pattern to redlining-era transmission-line routing that data centers now cluster around, from pollution complaints near xAI's Memphis turbines to a Taylor, Texas, park slated for a data center next to a Black neighborhood.
tech_top.pm_note: For anyone siting infrastructure, this is a preview of coming scrutiny: voters have already rejected data centers at the ballot box in some races, so equity impact and community engagement are becoming delivery constraints on a project timeline, not just PR considerations.

tech_top.headline: An Anthropic Mathematician Says He and Claude Solved the 167-Year-Old Riemann Hypothesis
tech_top.blurb: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he worked with Claude to produce a Lean-formalized proof of the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, and other mathematicians confirmed the formal proof compiles — though no one has yet produced a human-readable explanation of why it works. The claim arrived the same week a Stanford postdoc separately posted an unformalized, human-only proof of a generalized version, as the mathematical community works through both.
tech_top.pm_note: Formal verification let the field check a startling claim within days instead of months of peer review — a pattern worth borrowing for any AI-generated output in a domain where correctness can be checked mechanically, even though 'it compiles' and 'we understand it' remain two different things.

tech_more.headline: A Transcription Firm Used by Police and Prosecutors Left Interview Recordings and Bodycam Footage Exposed Online
tech_more.blurb: Security researcher Anurag Sen found that Tigerfish, a transcription company serving police departments and prosecutors, had left recordings, raw audio and customer invoices sitting unprotected on a public cloud storage bucket for weeks before the company secured it.

tech_more.headline: Bending Spoons Buys Mailchimp From Intuit for $3.68 Billion — a Steep Loss for Intuit
tech_more.blurb: Bending Spoons is buying Mailchimp from Intuit for $3.68 billion in a mostly-cash deal, a fraction of the roughly $12 billion Intuit paid for it in 2021, as Intuit refocuses on AI tools for small businesses. It's the latest in a buying spree that has brought AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable and Miro under Bending Spoons in the past year alone.

tech_101.text: The pattern where new infrastructure — like data centers — clusters in the same neighborhoods that historic, racially discriminatory redlining once shaped, often because it follows transmission lines or land that was cheap for the same underlying reasons. The 404 Media study found this pattern holds for data centers even after controlling for income and education.

A way of checking a mathematical proof by writing it in a language, like Lean, that software can verify step by step for logical validity. It can confirm a proof is internally consistent far faster than human peer review, but it doesn't by itself tell anyone why the proof works.

science.headline: Voyager 1 Is Now So Far Away a Signal Takes a Full Day to Reach It
science.blurb: NASA's Voyager 1, launched in 1977, has become the first spacecraft to sit a full light-day from Earth — about 16.1 billion miles away — so a radio signal now takes 24 hours each way. The nearly 50-year-old probe hasn't returned usable science data since November 14, and engineers are racing to restore its data flow while rationing a nuclear power supply expected to keep its remaining instruments running only until around summer 2027.

science.headline: A Chip Holding a Million Microcrystals Reveals Why Some Semiconductors Form Layered Cores and Shells
science.blurb: Northwestern chemists built a chip patterned with a million microscopic wells to rapidly map how cesium-based, lead-free semiconductor mixtures crystallize, finding that some recipes separate into bromine-rich cores wrapped in iodine-rich shells. The layered core structure explains why these materials sometimes have unexpectedly small bandgaps despite higher bromine content, and the bromine-rich regions also resisted humid-air degradation far better — a clue for building cheaper, more stable solar cells and LEDs.

science.headline: Bumblebees Solve Puzzles With Under a Million Neurons, Challenging Assumptions About Brain Size and Intelligence
science.blurb: Bumblebees, whose brains hold fewer than a million neurons, can move objects to reach nectar and learn to solve puzzles by watching other bees, and a review by two neuroscientists argues their oversized memory and navigation circuits — not bigger brains — explain it. The authors say sophisticated cognition may come from refined wiring rather than entirely new neural machinery, challenging the assumption that intelligence scales mainly with brain size.

philosophy.headline: What If Civilisation Was Built on Horseback, Not on Grain?
philosophy.blurb: Historian Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene argues the first states arose not from grain surpluses but from 'extrahuman transportation' — horses, boats, chariots — that let mobile pastoralists project power and conquer settled farming societies, from Bronze Age Sintashta to the Comanche. He traces the rival 'grain thesis' to a Cold War-era paradigm built to support territorial claims over Inner Asia, and argues it has wrongly erased the steppe's central role in building the earliest empires.

philosophy.headline: Astronomy Keeps Dismissing Its Strangest Discoveries as 'Nuisances' in the Hunt for Bigger Questions
philosophy.blurb: Physicist Dylan Jow argues that astronomy has been reorganized around fundamental physics' 'Big Questions' — dark energy, cosmic dawn — so interstellar dust and gas get treated as 'nuisances' to be subtracted away rather than studied for their own sake. He traces this hierarchy to Cold War-era funding shifts and the loss of the Superconducting Super Collider, arguing it's a historical accident rather than a natural order, and that reclaiming the 'nuisance' might restore astronomy's oldest appeal: wondering where we come from.

philosophy.headline: When an AI Companion Is the Only Thing That Remembers a Child's Day
philosophy.blurb: Psychoanalyst Tom Wooldridge argues the real question about children and AI companions isn't whether they displace human relationships, but what they offer the growing number of children with inadequate emotional support — and what they cannot. Drawing on attachment theory, he argues AI can approximate the consistency a child needs, but can never provide the mutuality of being refused and discovering another mind that exists independently of her wishes, leaving open what we owe the children it currently holds.

philosophy_101.text: The idea that early states arose when mobile, horse- or boat-enabled pastoralist groups conquered and ruled over settled farming populations, rather than farming itself producing the surplus that created states. It challenges the more familiar 'grain thesis,' which credits agricultural surplus with giving rise to the first governments.

Psychoanalyst Jessica Benjamin's idea that a real relationship requires two independent centers of experience, each affected by but not controlled by the other. Wooldridge argues an AI companion, however responsive, can't yet provide this — it is never changed by the child the way another person is.
